title: Quantum parallelism
myth: A quantum computer tries all answers at once
belief: Superposition lets a qubit be 0 and 1 simultaneously — so it feels natural to think the computer is checking every possible answer in parallel, like running millions of calculations at the same time. Pop science articles repeat this idea constantly.
correction: Superposition is not parallelism. Yes, a qubit can be in a superposition of states — but the moment you measure the result, the wavefunction collapses to a single classical outcome. If quantum computers truly tried all answers at once, you could just measure and get the right answer immediately. You cannot. The real work in quantum algorithms is engineering interference — carefully arranging the circuit so wrong answers cancel each other out and the correct answer amplitude grows. That is what Grover's algorithm does. That is what makes quantum algorithms hard to design.
researchNote: The precise computational model is the quantum circuit model operating on a Hilbert space of dimension 2^n. Quantum speedup comes from exploiting interference and entanglement, not classical parallelism. See Aaronson (2013) Quantum Computing Since Democritus for a rigorous treatment of what quantum computers can and cannot do. Nielsen and Chuang Chapter 1 also addresses this directly.
simulatorGuide: Load the Grover preset. First run it as-is and note the probability distribution — one answer is amplified. Then clear the circuit, place only H gates on both qubits, and simulate — you get equal probabilities. The Grover version amplifies one answer through interference, not by trying all answers.

title: What superposition actually means
myth: Superposition means a qubit is 0 and 1 at the same time
belief: The phrase both 0 and 1 simultaneously appears in almost every quantum computing explainer. It is a convenient shorthand that feels intuitive because it borrows from classical logic.
correction: A qubit in superposition is not simultaneously 0 and 1 in any classical sense. It is in a quantum state described by a complex linear combination: alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1. These amplitudes are not probabilities — they are complex numbers that can interfere. When you measure, you get 0 with probability |alpha|^2 or 1 with probability |beta|^2. Before measurement, the qubit does not have a definite value. Saying it is both at once imports classical intuition into a domain where it does not belong.
researchNote: The Copenhagen interpretation avoids assigning definite values before measurement. The many-worlds interpretation assigns all values in different branches. Neither maps to both 0 and 1 at once in the colloquial sense. The mathematical object is a unit vector in C^2. See Dirac (1930) The Principles of Quantum Mechanics for the original formulation.
simulatorGuide: Place a single H gate on q0. Switch to the Shot histogram tab and run with 1024 shots. You get roughly 50% zeros and 50% ones — random each time. Now add a second H gate after the first. Run again. You get 100% zeros. Two H gates cancel. That is interference, not two simultaneous values.

title: Entanglement and communication
myth: Entanglement allows faster-than-light communication
belief: Two entangled qubits seem connected regardless of distance. If measuring one instantly affects the other, it seems natural to use this as a communication channel faster than light.
correction: Measuring one entangled qubit does collapse the joint state instantly — but the outcome you get is random. You cannot control what result you get, so you cannot encode a message. The other party sees a random result too, with no way to tell whether your qubit was measured or not. This is the no-communication theorem. Entanglement enables quantum teleportation and superdense coding, but both require a classical channel alongside the entanglement — neither exceeds the speed of light.
researchNote: The no-communication theorem is a direct consequence of the linearity of quantum mechanics and the trace operation for partial measurements. See Nielsen and Chuang section 2.3. Bell inequalities confirm the correlations are real and non-local, but Eberhard (1978) proved non-local correlations cannot transmit information. Aspect et al. (1982) confirmed Bell inequality violations experimentally.
simulatorGuide: Load the Bell state preset and simulate. Notice the state is 50% |00> and 50% |11> — never |01> or |10>. Now add a measurement gate on q0 at step t2 and simulate multiple times. Every run, both qubits agree. But you cannot control which outcome you get — so you cannot send information.

title: The nature of quantum measurement
myth: Measurement just reads a pre-existing value
belief: Measurement in classical physics reads a property the system already had. A thermometer reads the temperature that was already there. It feels natural to assume quantum measurement works the same way.
correction: In quantum mechanics, measurement is not passive. It actively collapses the wavefunction — the act of measuring creates the definite outcome. Bell inequality experiments have proven that quantum systems do not have hidden pre-existing values. The outcome is genuinely random and only becomes definite at measurement. This is not a limitation of our knowledge — it is a fundamental feature of quantum mechanics confirmed experimentally.
researchNote: Bell (1964) showed that no local hidden variable theory can reproduce all quantum predictions. Aspect et al. (1982) confirmed this experimentally with photon polarization. The CHSH inequality provides a testable bound: classical correlations satisfy |S| <= 2, quantum mechanics achieves up to 2*sqrt(2) approximately 2.83. Loophole-free tests were completed by Hensen et al. (2015) in Nature.
simulatorGuide: Load the Measure demo preset. Run it 10 times. Each run collapses q0 differently — sometimes 0, sometimes 1. The result is not determined before measurement. Notice gates after M operate on the collapsed classical state.

title: Basis dependence
myth: The choice of measurement basis does not matter
belief: A bit is a bit — measuring in different ways should give the same information. Classical information does not depend on how you read it.
correction: In quantum mechanics, the choice of measurement basis fundamentally changes what information you extract. A qubit in state |+> = (|0> + |1>)/sqrt(2) gives completely random results in the computational basis, but gives a definite result in the Hadamard basis. Quantum information is basis-dependent. This is why quantum key distribution works — measuring in the wrong basis destroys the information rather than revealing it.
researchNote: The mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) formalism quantifies this. For a qubit, the computational basis {|0>, |1>} and the Hadamard basis {|+>, |->} are maximally incompatible — knowing the state in one basis gives zero information about outcomes in the other. This is the formal foundation of BB84 quantum key distribution (Bennett and Brassard, 1984).
simulatorGuide: Place H on q0, then Z, then H. Run it — you get |1> with 100% probability. Now remove the middle Z and run again — you get |0>. Same initial state, same final measurement, completely different result because of what happened in between. The basis transformation changed everything.

title: Qubit count vs performance
myth: More qubits always means better performance
belief: Classical computers get faster with more processors. More qubits sounds like more computational power — a natural extension of the classical intuition that bigger hardware is better hardware.
correction: Qubit count is one metric among many. A system with 1000 noisy qubits with poor connectivity and high error rates is far less useful than 50 high-quality qubits with low noise and full connectivity. What matters is the number of fault-tolerant logical qubits, circuit depth achievable before decoherence, two-qubit gate fidelity, qubit connectivity, and coherence time. IBM quantum volume and CLOPS metrics were developed precisely because raw qubit count is misleading.
researchNote: Quantum volume (Cross et al., 2019, IBM) is a composite metric that accounts for qubit count, connectivity, gate fidelity, and coherence time simultaneously. A device with 50 well-connected, low-noise qubits can have higher quantum volume than a 1000-qubit device with poor fidelity. CLOPS (circuit layer operations per second) measures throughput more practically.

title: The real cost of noise
myth: Noise only slightly affects quantum results
belief: A 1% error rate per gate sounds small. Classical computers tolerate noise too — error correcting codes in memory, checksums in storage. Surely a little quantum noise just slightly degrades results.
correction: Quantum noise is catastrophic in a way classical noise is not. A 1% depolarizing error per gate on a 100-gate circuit gives an overall fidelity of roughly 0.99^100 = 36%. The result is nearly useless. Classical bits can be copied and checked — quantum states cannot be cloned, so error correction requires enormous overhead. On NISQ devices with no error correction, even shallow circuits of a few dozen gates produce unreliable results.
researchNote: The threshold theorem (Aharonov and Ben-Or, 1997) states that fault-tolerant quantum computation is possible if the error rate per gate is below a threshold — roughly 1% for surface codes. Below threshold, adding more error correction qubits reduces the logical error rate exponentially. The surface code (Fowler et al., 2012) is the leading practical proposal, requiring roughly 1000 physical qubits per logical qubit at realistic error rates.
simulatorGuide: Load the Bell state. Simulate with noise at 0% — perfect 50/50. Now drag the noise slider to 5%, then 10%, then 20%. Watch the distribution degrade toward a uniform mixture. At 20% error per gate the Bell state is nearly destroyed after just 3 gates.

title: Decoherence vs noise
myth: Decoherence is just another word for noise
belief: Both decoherence and noise cause errors in quantum computations. They seem to describe the same problem — something going wrong with the qubits.
correction: Decoherence and noise are related but distinct. Decoherence is the loss of quantum coherence — the quantum phase relationships between basis states — due to interaction with the environment. It is a time-dependent process: a qubit left alone will decohere even without any gates being applied. Noise refers to errors introduced during gate operations. A circuit can fail due to decoherence even if every individual gate is perfect, simply because the circuit took too long to execute.
researchNote: T1 (relaxation time) measures how long a qubit stays in the excited state |1> before decaying to |0>. T2 (dephasing time) measures how long the phase coherence survives. T2 <= 2*T1 always. Modern superconducting qubits have T1 and T2 on the order of 100-500 microseconds. Gate times are typically 10-100 nanoseconds, so a circuit must complete in a time much less than T2 to maintain coherence.
simulatorGuide: Load the Bell state and gradually increase the noise slider. Each noise level approximates decoherence at a different timescale — higher noise represents a longer circuit relative to the coherence time. This is a simplified model; real decoherence is continuous and time-dependent.

title: Qubit connectivity constraints
myth: All qubits in a chip can interact directly
belief: In a quantum circuit diagram, any two qubits can be connected by a CNOT gate. It seems natural to assume the hardware implements this directly.
correction: Real quantum hardware has a fixed connectivity graph — only physically adjacent qubits can interact directly. On IBM devices this is a heavy-hex lattice. On Google Sycamore it is a 2D grid. To apply a gate between non-adjacent qubits, the compiler must insert SWAP gates to move the qubit states physically closer. Each SWAP requires 3 CNOT gates and adds significant noise. This qubit routing overhead can multiply the effective circuit depth by 2-5x on typical circuits.
researchNote: Qubit routing is an NP-hard optimization problem in general (Botea et al., 2018). Modern compilers use heuristic approaches — Qiskit uses a SABRE routing algorithm (Li et al., 2019). The heavy-hex topology used in IBM Eagle and Heron processors was specifically designed to reduce CNOT error rates by reducing crosstalk between adjacent qubits.

title: Quantum ML vs classical ML
myth: Quantum ML always beats classical ML
belief: Quantum computers are more powerful than classical ones. Machine learning benefits from more compute. Therefore quantum ML must be better than classical ML. This reasoning appears in many early QML papers.
correction: This reasoning has two flaws. First, quantum computers are not universally more powerful — they have specific advantages for specific problem structures. Second, classical ML has decades of optimization, hardware acceleration (GPUs, TPUs), and mature tooling. Huang et al. (2021) showed that for most classical datasets, classical kernel methods can match quantum kernel methods by constructing a classical kernel that mimics the quantum feature map. Quantum ML advantage requires problem structure that is genuinely hard to capture classically — and such structure is rare.
researchNote: The dequantization results by Tang (2019) and others showed that several proposed quantum ML speedups can be matched classically given quantum-inspired sampling access. Huang et al. (2021) Nature Communications proved that classical kernels can match quantum kernels on classical data. True quantum ML advantage likely requires either quantum data input or problems with provable classical hardness in BQP but not BPP.

title: Barren plateaus in VQA
myth: Barren plateaus are just a training trick to fix
belief: Gradient vanishing is a known problem in classical deep learning. It was fixed with batch normalization, residual connections, and better initialization. Surely the same class of solutions will fix barren plateaus in quantum circuits.
correction: Barren plateaus are fundamentally different from classical vanishing gradients. The gradient variance vanishes exponentially in the number of qubits — not just as a function of depth. For a global cost function on n qubits, the gradient magnitude scales as O(2^-n). No classical optimization trick fixes this because it is a consequence of the geometry of high-dimensional Hilbert space. Local cost functions partially mitigate this but introduce other trade-offs between trainability and expressiveness.
researchNote: McClean et al. (2018) Nature Communications proved the barren plateau theorem. Cerezo et al. (2021) showed cost-function dependence — local cost functions on shallow circuits avoid barren plateaus. Holmes et al. (2022) PRX Quantum connected barren plateaus to expressibility — highly expressive ansatze have flatter landscapes. This trainability-expressibility trade-off is a fundamental tension in VQA design with no known general solution.

title: Data encoding in QML
myth: Data encoding into qubits is straightforward
belief: Classical data is just numbers. Qubits store numbers. Feeding data into a quantum circuit should be as simple as setting qubit values.
correction: Data encoding is one of the most critical and underappreciated bottlenecks in QML. There is no single correct encoding — amplitude encoding, angle encoding, basis encoding, and IQP-style encoding each make different trade-offs between expressiveness, circuit depth, and the number of qubits required. Amplitude encoding can store 2^n values in n qubits but requires O(2^n) gates to prepare. Angle encoding uses fewer gates but wastes the exponential state space. The choice of encoding fundamentally shapes what the model can learn and whether any quantum advantage is possible.
researchNote: Schuld and Petruccione (2021) Quantum Models as Kernel Methods provides a unified view of encoding strategies. Goto et al. (2021) showed that the encoding defines an implicit kernel, connecting QML to kernel methods. The data re-uploading technique (Perez-Salinas et al., 2020) allows repeated encoding of the same data point at multiple circuit layers to increase expressiveness.
demoNote: Data encoding requires parameterized circuits with real dataset inputs — beyond what a browser simulator can demonstrate fairly. See the Schuld and Petruccione (2021) reference for a rigorous treatment.

title: Quantum kernel superiority
myth: Quantum kernels are always superior to classical kernels
belief: Quantum feature maps access exponentially large Hilbert spaces. Classical kernels cannot do this. Therefore quantum kernels must be more powerful than classical ones.
correction: Access to a large feature space is not sufficient for advantage. Huang et al. (2021) showed that for any quantum kernel, a classical kernel can be constructed that matches its performance on classical data, provided the classical kernel is given access to the quantum kernel values as training data. Quantum kernel advantage requires that the classification problem has structure that is hard to compute classically — which corresponds to problems in BQP but not BPP. Such problems are unlikely to appear naturally in standard ML benchmarks.
researchNote: Liu et al. (2021) Nature Physics provided a rigorous proof-of-principle quantum kernel advantage for a specific cryptography-inspired dataset. However, this dataset was artificially constructed. Kubler et al. (2021) showed that quantum kernels suffer from concentration — the kernel values become exponentially close to a constant as qubit count grows, making classification impossible without exponentially many samples.
demoNote: Kernel comparison requires training on real datasets with proper statistical evaluation. The Huang et al. (2021) paper linked in the research notes contains the definitive experimental comparison.

title: Scaling variational circuits
myth: Variational circuits will scale to useful problems soon
belief: VQCs are already showing promising results on small problems. As hardware improves and circuits get larger, they will naturally scale to industrially relevant problems in optimization, chemistry, and ML.
correction: VQCs face three simultaneous fundamental scaling challenges that do not diminish with hardware improvements alone. First, barren plateaus make training exponentially harder as qubit count grows. Second, noise accumulates faster than circuit depth can increase. Third, the classical simulation needed for gradient computation scales exponentially. These are not engineering challenges — they are algorithmic ones. Current VQC results on toy problems do not provide evidence of scalable quantum advantage.
researchNote: Cerezo et al. (2021) Nature Reviews Physics provides a comprehensive survey of VQA challenges. Stilck-Franca and Garcia-Patron (2021) proved that for random circuit problems, VQCs cannot outperform classical algorithms. The question of whether VQCs have any practical quantum advantage for real-world optimization remains open as of 2024.
simulatorGuide: Place Rx and Ry rotation gates on multiple qubits with different angles. Run and inspect the state vector. Notice how sensitive the output is to angle changes. Now increase noise to 5% and run 10 times — the results vary dramatically. This sensitivity combined with noise and barren plateaus is why scaling VQCs is extremely difficult.

title: How Grover search actually works
myth: Grover search works like a classical binary search
belief: Binary search is fast because it eliminates half the search space each step. Grover's algorithm searches a database quadratically faster than classical — it must work by a similar elimination process.
correction: Grover's algorithm achieves quadratic speedup through amplitude amplification — not elimination. It starts with equal superposition across all N states, then applies an oracle that flips the phase of the target state, followed by a diffusion operator that reflects all amplitudes around their average. This constructively interferes to increase the target amplitude and destructively interferes to decrease all others. After O(sqrt(N)) iterations the target has near-unit probability. There is no elimination — all states are present throughout.
researchNote: Bennett et al. (1997) proved that Grover's quadratic speedup is optimal — no quantum algorithm can search an unstructured database faster than O(sqrt(N)). The algorithm is tight. Unlike binary search where problem structure enables exponential improvements, Grover's applies to truly unstructured search where no classical algorithm beats O(N).
simulatorGuide: Load the Grover preset. Run it and look at the probability bars — |11> has much higher probability than the others. Now clear and place only H gates. Every state has equal probability. Grover does not eliminate wrong answers — it amplifies the right one through interference.

title: Shor's algorithm and encryption
myth: Shor algorithm will instantly break all encryption
belief: Shor's algorithm factors large numbers exponentially faster than classical computers. RSA encryption relies on factoring being hard. Therefore all encryption is immediately broken once quantum computers exist.
correction: Shor's algorithm requires millions of fault-tolerant logical qubits to break RSA-2048. Gidney and Ekera (2021) estimated breaking RSA-2048 requires approximately 20 million physical qubits running for 8 hours. Current best hardware has around 1000 physical qubits with much higher error rates than needed. Additionally, post-quantum cryptography standards were finalized by NIST in 2024 — CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium — and deployment has already begun.
researchNote: Gidney and Ekera (2021) Quantum journal provided the most rigorous current estimate: 20 million physical qubits with surface code error correction to break RSA-2048. Shor (1997) SIAM Journal is the original algorithm. NIST PQC standardization completed in 2024 with FIPS 203, 204, and 205 standards based on lattice cryptography.

title: Quantum teleportation
myth: Quantum teleportation moves matter instantly
belief: The word teleportation implies instant physical transport. Science fiction has made this association so strong that the quantum version is assumed to work the same way.
correction: Quantum teleportation transfers a quantum state — not matter, not energy, not information faster than light. It requires a pre-shared entangled pair plus two classical bits sent over a normal channel. The classical channel limits the speed to at most the speed of light. What is remarkable is that an unknown quantum state can be transferred without ever physically moving the qubit and without violating the no-cloning theorem — but this is not teleportation in the science fiction sense.
researchNote: Bennett et al. (1993) Physical Review Letters introduced quantum teleportation. The protocol requires 1 ebit of entanglement and 2 classical bits. It has been experimentally realized over distances exceeding 1400 km using satellite-based entanglement distribution (Ren et al., 2017 Nature). The no-cloning theorem (Wootters and Zurek, 1982) proves that teleportation must destroy the original state.
simulatorGuide: Load the Teleportation preset. Notice it uses 3 qubits and requires CNOT gates — a classical channel is embedded in the protocol. The state of q0 is transferred to q2, but only after classical information flows through the circuit. Run it multiple times — the outcome varies because measurement is involved.

title: The scope of quantum speedup
myth: Quantum speedup applies to every problem
belief: Quantum computers are more powerful than classical ones. Therefore they should be faster at everything — sorting, searching, optimization, machine learning, simulation.
correction: Quantum speedup applies to a specific and limited class of problems. Grover's algorithm gives quadratic speedup for unstructured search. Shor's gives exponential speedup for factoring. HHL gives exponential speedup for linear systems under strong conditions. But for most practically important problems — general optimization, neural network training, data analytics — no quantum speedup is known, and for many there are lower bound proofs showing no substantial speedup is possible. The problems where quantum computers excel are structurally different from everyday computing tasks.
researchNote: The quantum complexity zoo (quantumcomputingpatterns.com) catalogs known quantum speedups. Aaronson and Ambainis (2009) proved that quantum speedup for black-box problems requires the problem to have specific algebraic structure. For NP-complete problems, quantum computers provide at most quadratic speedup via Grover — not exponential.
simulatorGuide: Run the Grover preset and note the quadratic speedup: 2 qubits means 4 possible states, Grover finds the answer in O(sqrt(4)) = 2 iterations instead of 4. Now think about what this means for a 50-qubit system: sqrt(2^50) iterations instead of 2^50. That is a speedup, but it is quadratic not exponential — and it only applies when you have an oracle for the target.

title: Circuit depth and power
myth: A deeper circuit is always more powerful
belief: More layers in a neural network generally means more expressive power. The same logic seems to apply to quantum circuits — more gates should mean more capability.
correction: On NISQ hardware, deeper circuits accumulate more noise and often produce less reliable results than shallower ones. Beyond noise, circuit depth increases execution time, which must remain shorter than the qubit coherence time. There is also the barren plateau problem — deeper parametrized circuits tend to have flatter optimization landscapes. The right circuit depth is the minimum needed for the task, not the maximum possible.
researchNote: Circuit depth is measured as the longest path from input to output through the directed acyclic graph of gates. The critical depth is device-specific — determined by the ratio of gate time to coherence time. For superconducting qubits, a gate takes roughly 50ns and coherence time is roughly 100 microseconds, allowing roughly 2000 sequential gates before coherence is lost. Two-qubit gates are typically 3-10x slower than single-qubit gates.
simulatorGuide: Load the Interference preset (H-Z-H). This achieves X in depth 3. Now try adding more H and Z gates after — the result does not change because H-Z-H already implements X exactly. Extra depth adds nothing here except noise on real hardware.

title: Quantum gate reversibility
myth: Quantum gates can be irreversible just like classical gates
belief: Classical computing uses irreversible gates like AND and OR — information is destroyed. Quantum gates seem similar so they might also be irreversible.
correction: All quantum gates — without measurement — must be reversible. This is a consequence of unitarity: quantum evolution is described by unitary matrices, and every unitary matrix has an inverse. AND and OR are irreversible classically because they map 2 bits to 1 bit, losing information. Quantum gates always map n qubits to n qubits. The Toffoli gate (CCX) proves that any classical computation can be made reversible with at most a constant overhead. Irreversibility only enters quantum computing through measurement.
researchNote: Landauer (1961) showed that irreversible classical computation must dissipate energy (Landauer's principle). Bennett (1973) showed that reversible computation can avoid this energy cost. The quantum circuit model inherits reversibility from unitary evolution — every quantum gate U has inverse U-dagger. This is why quantum error correction is possible: errors are unitary and can be corrected.
simulatorGuide: Build any circuit, then add the exact reverse — each gate applied in reverse order. Run it and observe that you always recover |00...0>. Quantum gates are reversible by construction. Try H then H (equals identity), or CNOT then CNOT (equals identity). Every gate undoes itself.

title: Circuit expressibility
myth: A bigger circuit is always more expressive
belief: More gates means more operations means more things the circuit can compute. Adding gates to a circuit should always increase what states it can reach.
correction: Expressibility — the ability to reach a diverse set of states — does not increase monotonically with circuit size. H followed by H is the identity. CNOT followed by CNOT is the identity. Adding redundant gates reduces expressibility per gate while increasing depth and noise. Furthermore, for parametrized circuits, high expressibility correlates with barren plateaus — circuits that can reach any state have exponentially flat loss landscapes and cannot be trained. The optimal circuit is the smallest one that can express the target state, not the largest.
researchNote: Sim et al. (2019) Advanced Quantum Technologies introduced quantitative expressibility measures based on the deviation of the output state distribution from the Haar random distribution. They showed a fundamental trade-off: circuits with high expressibility tend to have worse trainability. This is directly related to the barren plateau results of McClean et al. (2018).
simulatorGuide: Build two circuits of the same depth — one with only X and Z gates, one mixing H, Rx, CNOT. Run both and compare the state vectors. The second reaches states the first cannot. But try H+H on the same qubit — they cancel completely. More gates does not always mean more expressiveness.

title: CNOT and entanglement
myth: CNOT gate creates entanglement on its own
belief: CNOT is the standard two-qubit entangling gate. It is used to create Bell states. So it must create entanglement whenever it is applied.
correction: CNOT does not always create entanglement. If the control qubit is in a computational basis state (|0> or |1>) rather than superposition, CNOT acts as a classical conditional flip — no entanglement is created. Entanglement requires a superposition on the control qubit before the CNOT. The standard Bell state preparation works because H creates superposition first, then CNOT correlates the two qubits. A CNOT on |00> simply gives |00> — no entanglement.
researchNote: Entanglement is a property of the joint quantum state, not of any individual gate. A state |psi_AB> is entangled if and only if it cannot be written as a product state |psi_A> tensor |psi_B>. The entangling power of CNOT — measured as the average entanglement generated over Haar-random input states — is non-zero, but CNOT can also map separable states to separable states depending on the input.
simulatorGuide: First run the Bell state (H then CNOT) — you get entanglement, 50% |00> and 50% |11>. Now remove the H gate and run CNOT alone on |00>. You get |00> with 100% probability — no entanglement. The H gate is what creates the superposition that CNOT then entangles.

title: Classical vs quantum gates
myth: Any classical gate has a direct quantum equivalent
belief: Classical computing uses AND, OR, NOT, XOR. Quantum computing has X (NOT), CNOT (controlled-NOT), and Toffoli (AND). The mapping seems direct.
correction: Classical gates and quantum gates differ in a fundamental way: classical gates can be irreversible (AND, OR lose information), while all quantum gates except measurement must be unitary and therefore reversible. A classical AND gate maps 4 inputs to 2 outputs — this information loss cannot be represented as a unitary matrix. The Toffoli gate simulates AND reversibly by keeping all input bits and adding an output bit. Additionally, quantum gates include operations with no classical equivalent — Hadamard, phase gates, and rotations that create and manipulate superposition.
researchNote: The Toffoli gate (Toffoli, 1980) proved that reversible classical computation is universal. The Hadamard and T gates, combined with CNOT, form a universal gate set for quantum computation (Boykin et al., 1999). There is no classical equivalent of the Hadamard gate — it is intrinsically quantum, creating superposition from a basis state.
simulatorGuide: Place an H gate on q0 and run it. The output is a superposition — no classical bit operation does this. Now place H then Z then H — the result is X (bit flip). This H-Z-H sequence has no direct classical analog; it works through quantum interference of amplitudes.

title: Wave-particle duality
myth: Quantum objects are sometimes waves and sometimes particles
belief: The double-slit experiment shows interference (wave behavior) but photon detectors click discretely (particle behavior). It sounds natural to say light switches between the two depending on the situation.
correction: Quantum objects are neither waves nor particles in the classical sense — they are quantum objects that have no classical analog. The wave-particle language is a historical accident from trying to describe quantum phenomena using classical concepts. The wavefunction is not a physical wave of anything — it is a probability amplitude. When we say light behaves like a wave, we mean its probability amplitudes interfere. When we say it behaves like a particle, we mean measurements give discrete outcomes. It does not switch — it is always quantum.
researchNote: Feynman (1965) Lectures on Physics Vol. 3 opens with the double-slit experiment and explicitly warns against the wave-particle duality framing. The modern understanding is that quantum mechanics is a single consistent framework — the apparent duality reflects the limitations of classical intuition, not properties of the quantum object itself.
simulatorGuide: Load the Interference preset. H-Z-H = X shows quantum interference of probability amplitudes — the |0> amplitude and |1> amplitude cancel completely. This is not a wave phenomenon in the classical sense — it is interference of complex numbers in Hilbert space. Run it and see 100% probability of |1>.

title: Quantum supremacy means useful advantage
myth: Quantum supremacy means quantum computers are now better than classical
belief: Google announced quantum supremacy in 2019. Supremacy sounds like a decisive victory — quantum computers are now superior to classical ones for computation.
correction: Quantum supremacy (now often called quantum advantage) means a quantum device completed one specific task faster than the best known classical algorithm for that task. The task — random circuit sampling — has no known practical application. It was specifically designed to be hard for classical computers and easy for quantum ones. Classical supercomputers have since improved their simulation algorithms and reduced the estimated classical runtime dramatically. Supremacy for one contrived task does not mean quantum computers are generally better.
researchNote: Arute et al. (2019) Nature claimed 10,000 years classical runtime. IBM disputed this within days, claiming optimized classical simulation could do it in 2.5 days. Pan et al. (2022) demonstrated classical simulation of random circuit sampling at comparable scales using tensor networks. The term quantum supremacy was replaced by quantum advantage in most literature to avoid the misleading connotation.
demoNote: Random circuit sampling requires hundreds of qubits to demonstrate — beyond browser simulation. The key lesson is about interpreting benchmark claims, not about circuit construction.

title: What quantum volume actually measures
myth: Quantum volume is just a marketing metric with no scientific meaning
belief: IBM invented quantum volume and only IBM devices score well on it. It sounds like a self-serving metric designed to make IBM hardware look good rather than an objective measure of capability.
correction: Quantum volume is a rigorous composite metric defined in a peer-reviewed paper (Cross et al., 2019). It measures the largest random square circuit a device can execute with greater than 2/3 probability of success. A circuit of depth d on d qubits tests qubit count, connectivity, gate fidelity, and coherence time simultaneously. QV doubles only when all four improve together. IonQ and Quantinuum trapped-ion devices routinely score higher QV than IBM superconducting devices despite having far fewer qubits — which proves it is not an IBM-favoring metric.
researchNote: Cross, A. W. et al. (2019) IBM Research defined quantum volume. The protocol involves random two-qubit gate circuits of increasing size. A device achieves QV=2^n if it can execute n-qubit random circuits with heavy output probability > 2/3. Quantinuum H2 processor achieved QV > 1,000,000 in 2023 with only 32 qubits, demonstrating that qubit quality dominates qubit count.

title: The no-cloning theorem
myth: You can copy a quantum state just like copying a classical bit
belief: Copying information is fundamental to classical computing — RAM, cache, registers all copy bits constantly. Quantum computers store information in qubits, so copying qubit states should work the same way.
correction: The no-cloning theorem (Wootters and Zurek, 1982) proves that it is physically impossible to create a perfect copy of an unknown quantum state. This follows directly from the linearity of quantum mechanics. If a cloning machine could copy |0> and |1>, linearity requires it to map (|0> + |1>)/sqrt(2) to a product of two copies — but that product state is not the same as the entangled state the linearity would produce. No-cloning is not a hardware limitation — it is a law of physics with deep implications for quantum error correction and cryptography.
researchNote: Wootters, W. K., Zurek, W. H. (1982) Nature proved no-cloning. The theorem is equivalent to the second law of quantum information. It makes quantum error correction non-trivial — you cannot just copy the qubit and take a majority vote. Instead, quantum error correction encodes logical qubits across many physical qubits using entanglement. No-cloning also underlies the security of quantum key distribution.
simulatorGuide: Try to build a circuit that copies q0 to q1 — starting from |00> make q1 match q0 for any input state. You will find CNOT copies |0> to |0> and |1> to |1> but fails for superposition states. Load Bell state and notice the output is an entangled state, not two identical copies of q0.

title: The HHL algorithm speedup
myth: HHL gives exponential speedup for solving linear systems
belief: The HHL algorithm (Harrow, Hassidim, Lloyd 2009) solves linear systems Ax=b in O(log N) time versus O(N) classically. An exponential speedup for one of the most fundamental problems in computational science — this must be transformative for science and engineering.
correction: The HHL speedup comes with severe conditions that eliminate practical utility in most cases. First, the input vector b must be loaded into quantum memory in O(log N) time — but reading N classical data points to prepare this state takes O(N) time, erasing the speedup. Second, the output is a quantum state — reading out all N components takes O(N) measurements. Third, the matrix A must be sparse and well-conditioned. Fourth, you need quantum RAM (not yet built). Under these conditions, HHL gives exponential speedup only in a narrow regime unlikely to match real-world problems.
researchNote: Harrow, Hassidim, Lloyd (2009) Physical Review Letters introduced HHL. Aaronson (2015) Nat. Physics wrote a critique called 'Read the fine print' explaining why HHL's conditions make practical speedup unlikely. Tang (2019) dequantized the recommendation system algorithm (inspired by HHL), showing classical algorithms can match it given quantum-like data access. The input/output problem is a fundamental barrier for most quantum linear algebra algorithms.
demoNote: HHL requires phase estimation and amplitude amplification circuits far beyond 4 qubits to demonstrate meaningfully. The key lesson is about reading fine print in speedup claims, not circuit construction.

title: Quantum annealing vs gate-based quantum computing
myth: D-Wave quantum annealers are the same as gate-based quantum computers
belief: D-Wave sells quantum computers with thousands of qubits. Gate-based quantum computers have far fewer. D-Wave must be more powerful since it has more qubits.
correction: D-Wave quantum annealers and gate-based quantum computers (IBM, Google, IonQ) are fundamentally different architectures solving different problems. Annealers are analog devices that physically implement optimization by slowly cooling a quantum system to its ground state — they can only solve certain optimization problems in this specific way. Gate-based computers are universal — they can run any quantum algorithm including Shor's and Grover's. D-Wave qubits have very short coherence times, very low connectivity, and cannot run general quantum circuits. The qubit counts are not comparable.
researchNote: Kadowaki and Nishimori (1998) introduced quantum annealing theoretically. D-Wave systems are adiabatic quantum computers — they implement the adiabatic theorem rather than the gate model. Ronnow et al. (2014) Science showed D-Wave offered no speedup over classical simulated annealing on benchmark problems. McGeoch and Wang (2013) showed speedup on specific D-Wave-native problems but not general optimization.
demoNote: Quantum annealing requires analog continuous-time simulation — not representable as a discrete gate circuit. The distinction is architectural and conceptual rather than demonstrable in a gate simulator.
